examples: No sooner do I teach something than the students forget it.
No sooner do I tidy up than the kids mess up the room again.
As soon as I delete an email, a new notification comes in.
I feel pathetic forgetting the content as soon as I read it.
As soon as I get my paycheck, it disappears into expenses.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to emphasize an annoying repetition, not simply "right after."
The second clause is usually something undesirable/negative; the speaker is in a complaining mood.
Not used for natural changes that happen once, such as:春になると桜が咲く（does not fit ～そばから）.

• "No sooner has … been done than … (again)", and this happens over and over.
• Emphasizes a feeling of helplessness/frustration because the action in the first clause is immediately "undone" by the second clause.
• Not used for one-time, ordinary natural events (non-repeating); it is usually a situation that keeps repeating.
fields.notes:
• In everyday expression, ～たそばから appears quite often (給料をもらったそばから). However, V-るそばから is the standard form.
• Fits pairs of verbs of "getting something done" vs "having it undone again": 片付ける⇔散らかす, 入力する⇔エラーが出る, 修理する⇔壊れる.
• The emphasis is stronger when combined with adverbs: 次から次へと／どんどん／また.
mistakes: Using it for a one-off event → incorrect; the JLPT often sets traps with non-repeating situations.
Choosing the wrong tense: many materials prefer V-るそばから; V-た also exists but is less "textbook."
If the second clause does not have the sense of "happening again right away" → it does not fit; you need the feeling of being immediately "overridden."

rows: As soon as you do it, … (again); repeated
Emphasizes recurrence, a nuance of dissatisfaction
<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>うそばから<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れる。
Emphasizes immediacy, once; no repetition required
<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がったとたん、めまいがした。
Overlapping moments; repeated or not, either is fine
<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>くか<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>かないかのうちに<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>り<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>した。
Formal, immediate; no implication of repetition
ベルが<ruby>鳴<rt>な</rt></ruby>るや<ruby>否<rt>いな</rt></ruby>や、<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>飛<rt>と</rt></ruby>び<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>した。

examples: Once you lend him money, it will never come back.
Some people, once they get involved in gambling, see their lives go downhill.
Once you believe that rumor, you can no longer judge him fairly.
Once you allow them to be spoiled, children become endlessly selfish.
Once I start drinking, even a sip, I can't stop.
Once you set foot in this industry, you can't easily get out.
fields.explain:
Strong, formal nuance; used for warnings/serious consequences.
The second clause is usually an inevitable reality beyond one's control; avoid using it with volition/direct commands.
Often accompanied by emphatic adverbs: いったん,一度, ひとたび.
Rarely used in casual everyday conversation; replaced by ～たら最後in spoken language.
Does not combine well with clearly positive content (sounds forced).

The pattern ～たが最後 expresses: "Once you have done V, the (consequence) is an unavoidable/irreversible outcome that drags on." Strong nuance, written language/speeches, often used to warn or to emphasize irreversibility.
• Meaning frame: trigger point -> one-way road -> fixed consequence (usually bad).
• The second clause often goes with expressions that close off the possibility of reversal: 二度と～ない, ～っぱなし, ～きり, もはや～ない.
• Often used with addictive/risky behavior: 手を出す, 足を踏み入れる, 口を出す, 付き合う, 借りる.
• Compared with ～たら最後: ～たが最後 is more formal and literary; the emphasis is usually stronger.
fields.notes:
• Often used in argumentative writing, news, and descriptions of risk: 依存・中毒・借金・噂・暴力など.
• Verb choices suggest "slipping into" something: 足を踏み入れる, 手を出す, 首を突っ込む, 甘える.
• The second clause often takes a lasting-state form: ～続ける, ～っぱなし, ～きり, ～まま.
• In journalism/headlines, the subject can be omitted to make it more general.
mistakes: Using it for a clearly positive result → unnatural. Use it with negative/hard-to-reverse consequences.
Using volition/a direct command in the second clause (～なさい/～してください) → wrong nuance.
Mistaking the time label for ～たとたん: ～たが最後 does not mean "right after" but "there is no going back."
Confusing it with ～以上(は)/～からには: those two patterns express obligation/a rule and do not imply "a point of no return."
JLPT trap: an answer choice with keywords like 二度と/～っぱなし/～きり alongside ～たが最後 is a sign it is correct.

rows: Once you have…, there is no way back
More colloquial than ～たが<ruby>最後<rt>さいご</rt></ruby>; the emphasis may be lighter
<ruby>借<rt>か</rt></ruby>りたら<ruby>最後<rt>さいご</rt></ruby>、<ruby>返<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ってこない。
Meaning of obligation/rule; not an inevitable outcome
<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>き<ruby>受<rt>う</rt></ruby>けた<ruby>以上<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>最後<rt>さいご</rt></ruby>までやる。
やるからには<ruby>全力<rt>ぜんりょく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>尽<rt>つ</rt></ruby>くす。
Closeness in time; no sense of "no going back"
<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がったとたん、めまいがした。
Succession in time, not a fixed outcome
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ったかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと、やんだ。

examples: Please pretend you didn't hear my slip of the tongue a moment ago.
Please count me as present today. I'll explain the reason for my absence later.
Please treat this email as if it never arrived. It was sent by mistake.
Please treat the details as undisclosed.
Please consider today's meeting as not having happened. The materials won't be ready in time.
Please make it so that I was the one who said this. I'll take responsibility.
fields.explain:
Polite, softens a request; implies hoping the listener will be understanding/cover for you.
Often used with verbs of perception:聞く,見る,受け取る,連絡する,報告する.
In official documents, it can be replaced with ～ということにお願いいたします (keigo).
Avoid overusing it in situations that call for transparency; it can give the impression of "covering something up."

The pattern ～たことにしてください expresses a polite request/suggestion: "Please treat (X) as having happened/not having happened." It is the polite imperative variant of ～たことにする (deciding for oneself to treat something as…), used to ask the listener to join in a "hypothetical agreement."
• Social function: soothing, avoiding conflict, saving face.
• Used a lot in the workplace, polite emails, and internal notices.
• Two main directions: overlooking a mistake (～なかったことにしてください) and provisional acknowledgment (～たことにしてください).
• Different from "～てください": it does not request an actual action, but a way of "viewing/recording" something.
fields.notes:
• In business emails: 〜いただけますと幸いです/〜お願いできますでしょうか to increase politeness.
• With sensitive content (コンプラ), avoid revealing an intent to "conceal"; use procedural wording instead.
• Pragmatics: reflects the "negative politeness" strategy (reducing pressure on the other party).
• To emphasize that "there is agreement," add: ご承知おきください/ご了承のほど.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～てください: that one requests an "action," while ～たことにしてください requests a "way of viewing/recording."
Using it for things that cannot be supposed (legal facts, mandatory figures) → pragmatically incorrect.
Missing agent/target: the context must make clear who is doing the "treating as."
JLPT trap: the correct answer often goes with 聞く/見る/連絡する/報告する and the negative なかったことにしてください.

rows: Deciding for yourself to treat it as having…
The agent is the speaker; not a request to someone else
<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>んだことにする。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>とは<ruby>他人<rt>たにん</rt></ruby>ということにしている。
<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>休業<rt>きゅうぎょう</rt></ruby>とする。
Acting as if you had… (in order to do something)
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったつもりで<ruby>貯金<rt>ちょきん</rt></ruby>する。
～ということにしてください
Form that assigns a nominalized clause
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>ということにしてください。

fields.meaning: There would be no end to it
examples: There'd be no end to it if I listed all the flaws, so let's stop here.
Once you start worrying, there's no end to it. Let's just try it first.
If you start wanting more, there's no end to it.
The same mistakes keep happening, so many that there'd be no end to listing examples.
If you start fussing over small details, there's no end to it.
There'd be no end to it if I counted up my complaints, but there is also a lot to be grateful for.
fields.explain:
Used to "wrap up" a topic and avoid going on too long: ～から、このへんで/やめよう/切り上げよう.
The tone is usually casual to neutral; suitable for conversation and commentary.
The first clause often uses Vます語幹 + 出す/始める to suggest a beginning:言い 出す ,数え 上げる .
Combines well with degree complements: ～ほど/～くらい.

The pattern ～たらきりがない expresses: "If you (say/list/worry/demand…), it will be endless, with no end in sight." Often used to close a topic, stop getting carried away, or emphasize how endless a problem is.
• "きりがない" = "there is no boundary/stopping point."
• Emphasizes endlessness in listing, worrying, or wanting.
• Often appears after verbs that open up a series: 言い出す, 挙げる, 数え上げる, こだわる, 心配する.
fields.notes:
• In presentations, used as a time-management strategy: 例を挙げたらきりがないので要点だけにします。
• In counseling/psychology, effective for stopping an endless cycle of anxiety: 心配し始めたらきりがないから、今できることに集中しよう。
• For it to sound natural, the verb before たら should be an action that "opens a list/process."
mistakes: Using it with verbs that do not suggest an "endless series" (such as 着く, 終える) → sounds forced.
Confusing "きり" with "切り" meaning "ending" → here it means "限り/boundary."
Dropping "たら" to make "たらない" → wrong meaning. It must be "Vたら + きりがない."
JLPT trap: set phrases like 挙げたら/言い出したら/数え上げたら with きりがない are a strong hint.

rows: If you do it, there is no stopping point
Has a nuance of concluding/wrapping up
<ruby>言<rt>いいだし</rt></ruby>い<ruby>出<rt></rt></ruby>したらきりがない。
If you do it, it is limitless
<ruby>要求<rt>ようきゅう</rt></ruby>しだしたら<ruby>際限<rt>さいげん</rt></ruby>がない。
いくら～てもきりがない
No matter how much, it is never enough
いくら<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>してもきりがない。
<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>には<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>りがある。

examples: Once you start playing smartphone games, you won't be able to stop spending money on them.
If you tell him a secret, it'll spread right away.
Once you start slacking off, it becomes a habit.
Once you run a tab at that place, you'll never be able to pay it back.
Once I start eating sweets, I can't stop.
Once you jump on a careless rumor, you lose people's trust.
fields.explain:
Colloquial, natural in conversation; the emphasis is still strong.
The second clause should be a negative, lasting, hard-to-fix consequence.
Combines well with emphatic complements: いったん/一度/ひとたび.
Avoid using it with clearly positive content (sounds contradictory).

～たら最後 expresses "once you have done…, it's all over; a bad consequence is inevitable and hard to reverse." It is the colloquial variant of ～たが最後. Used a lot in conversation to warn or to complain.
• Emphasizes the "point of no return."
• Often used with bad habits/addiction/danger: 飲みだす, 手を出す, さぼる, 嘘をつく.
• The second clause carries a nuance of helplessness/fate: もう～ない, もはや～ない, ずっと～まま.
fields.notes:
• Effective in admonishing advice: ～したら最後だよ (a casual warning).
• In health/education campaigns: 依存の怖さを強調するフレーズとして有効.
• Co-occurs with もう/二度と/もはや/ずっと to reinforce "no going back."
mistakes: Using it with a positive result → unnatural. Tie it to a bad/hard-to-reverse outcome.
A command/direct volition in the second clause → wrong nuance (it should describe an inevitable reality).
Confusing it with ～たとたん (only immediacy, without the meaning of a "point of no return").
JLPT trap: look for signs like 二度と/もう～ない/～っぱなし/～きり together with ～たら最後.

rows: Once you have…, there is no way back
Colloquial; equivalent to ~たが<ruby>最後<rt>さいご</rt></ruby>
<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>みだしたら<ruby>最後<rt>さいご</rt></ruby>、<ruby>止<rt>と</rt></ruby>まらない。
Once you have…, the outcome is inevitable
<ruby>手<rt>て</rt></ruby>を<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>したが<ruby>最後<rt>さいご</rt></ruby>、<ruby>破滅<rt>はめつ</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>き<ruby>受<rt>う</rt></ruby>けた<ruby>以上<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>、やり<ruby>遂<rt>と</rt></ruby>げる。

examples: If it rains, well, there are ways to enjoy the rain too.
If you don't have money, then you just have to make do without it.
If it's expensive, well, at least you can trust the quality.
If I go, I'll get busy, and if I don't go, people will worry about me.
With children, if they're quiet, you worry, and if they're noisy, it's exhausting.
When I do have time, I just end up slacking off.
fields.explain:
Creates a rhythm by repeating the word, expressing a "deal with it as it comes" attitude or that "either way has its difficulties."
Often used in contrasting pairs:行ったら…行かなかったら…, あるならあるで…ないならないで…
Does not emphasize a condition leading to a necessity; it is everyday commentary/remarks.
Casual to neutral; can be used in spoken language and light written language.

The pattern ～たら～たで states that even if A happens, "in situation A" there are also its own ways of dealing with it/difficulties. Used to express an attitude: not worrying too much, or that each option has its corresponding problems.
• Two common nuances:

Neutral/accepting: "it's fine either way; it will be handled in its own way."
Pointing out that both sides have drawbacks: "either way has its own hardship."

• Neutral/accepting: "it's fine either way; it will be handled in its own way."
• Pointing out that both sides have drawbacks: "either way has its own hardship."
• The second clause often contains a description of a specific consequence: "～なりの問題/メリット・デメリット".
• With Na/N, use なら～で; do not use だったら～だったで in standard written language.
fields.notes:
• A rhythmic pattern that is easy to use in advertising/sales: 高かったら高かったで価値がある.
• Can be chained to emphasize that "either way is hard": ～したらしたで…, しなかったらしなかったで…
• For the negative, ないならないで/なかったらなかったで is more natural than じゃないならじゃないで.
mistakes: Using だったら～だったで with Na/N in standard written language → use なら～で instead.
Mistaking it for a necessary condition like ～ならば → wrong nuance; this is a comment on "in that situation."
Dropping the repeated stem in the second part → incorrect pattern. Keep the same word: 高かったら高かったで.
JLPT trap: the correct answer often has the matching pair "あるならあるで／ないならないで".

rows: X たら X たで
Situation X also has its own ways/problems
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>かったら<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>かったで<ruby>安心<rt>あんしん</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>なら<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>楽<rt>たの</rt></ruby>しむ。
General concessive condition, no repetitive rhythm
No matter how much you…, still…
Emphasizes repeating an action; different purpose
<ruby>探<rt>さが</rt></ruby>しても<ruby>探<rt>さが</rt></ruby>しても<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>つからない。
<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいわ<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいで<ruby>大変<rt>たいへん</rt></ruby>。

examples: During important business negotiations, you must not let your guard down for even a second.
Not a single yen of research funds may be used for personal purposes.
In this project, we cannot afford to be missing even one person.
You mustn't skip training for even a single day.
This document is top secret. Not a single word may be leaked outside.
His eyes are like those of a hawk stalking its prey; he doesn't miss even an instant.
fields.explain:
Placed with the smallest unit to emphasize "absolutely not."
Combines naturally with:一秒・一分・一瞬・一滴・一円・一人・一言・一日…
Often used with a prohibition clause (～てはならない／いけない) or a negative of ability (～できない／ない).

• Emphasizes an absolute degree: "not even a single … / must not even one …."
• Usually combined with the smallest number, expressing strictness, discipline, vigilance.
• Stiff, formal style; often used in regulations and official speeches.
fields.notes:
• After たりとも comes the scope being negated; a negative form is needed at the end of the sentence.
• Not used with large or indefinite quantities (× 何人たりとも in the sense of "anyone" is incorrect in this pattern).
• In everyday spoken language, it can be replaced with "一秒も/一円も～ない".
mistakes: Forgetting the negative at the end of the sentence: × 一円たりとも無駄に → it must have 無駄にしない.
Using it with an abstract noun that is not a minimal unit: × 勇気たりともない (unnatural).
Wrong word order: × たりとも一秒 → it must be 一秒たりとも.

rows: Strong, formal, tied to a minimal unit
<ruby>一<rt>いち</rt></ruby><ruby>円<rt>えん</rt></ruby>たりとも<ruby>無駄<rt>むだ</rt></ruby>にしない
Lower degree of emphasis; no minimal unit required
General negation, no reference unit stated
まったく<ruby>覚<rt>おぼ</rt></ruby>えていない

examples: Anyone who is a leader must be fair.
As a doctor, one should always keep learning the latest knowledge.
As a working adult, it goes without saying that you should be punctual.
Act with awareness of the responsibility that comes with being a teacher.
Parents should not take out their emotions in front of their children.
As a researcher, he made data transparency his top priority.
fields.explain:
Used to emphasize standards of conduct appropriate to one's role/position.
Formal style: speeches, rules, writing on professional ethics.
Rarely used with ordinary/overly specific roles; avoid in casual conversation.

• States a role/position and the corresponding requirements, qualities, and responsibilities: "if you are …, then …."
• Formal, didactic nuance; often used with roles that carry status/moral weight (指導者・医師・社会人・親・教師…).
• Close in meaning to "としての/にふさわしい" but more archaic and stronger.
fields.notes:
• "者/もの/身/責任/使命/役割" are nouns that often go with "たる".
• "社会人たるもの" is a very common set phrase in company instructions.
• "たる" is not used before verbs; it attaches to a noun to form a noun phrase.
Do not merge with ～足る～ (): a different point (N+たる+N "as a" vs Vる+に足る "worthy of") — homophones once written in kana.
mistakes: Using it for inanimate objects/things: × 高級車たるエンジン (unnatural).
Using it in casual conversation makes the sentence sound pompous and overly archaic.
Wrong order: × たる指導者者 → it must be 指導者たる者.

rows: <ruby>医師<rt>いし</rt></ruby>としての<ruby>責任<rt>せきにん</rt></ruby>
An evaluation of suitability, not admonishing
<ruby>指導<rt>しどう</rt></ruby><ruby>者<rt>しゃ</rt></ruby>にふさわしい<ruby>態度<rt>たいど</rt></ruby>
<ruby>大人<rt>おとな</rt></ruby>らしい<ruby>行動<rt>こうどう</rt></ruby>
